
# MPX NYC Organizing


The RESPND-MI investigator group was grounded in a set of guiding goals and organized into core functions that structured its activities. Together, these principles and functions ensured that work was carried out effectively, inclusively, and with the resilience required during the mpox emergency.  

## Principles {.unnumbered}

The group’s work was guided by five key principles. Participation was meant to bring joy rather than stress, so that contributors felt energized by their involvement. The group embraced low-stakes failure, understanding experimentation and mistakes as an essential part of collective problem-solving. Efforts were designed to reflect abundance and redundancy, with overlapping initiatives seen not as wasteful but as a vital source of resilience. Commitment to democracy meant that decisions were made collectively and transparently, ensuring broad ownership of outcomes. Finally, the group built as it flew, adopting an iterative and adaptive approach that was responsive to the evolving conditions of the emergency.  

## Functions {.unnumbered}


The work of the investigator group was organized around four core functions. 

### Coordination {.unnumbered}
The first, coordination, focused on gathering and sharing information about the health emergency with stakeholders. This work included documenting the experiences of community-based organizations and city agencies, aligning programmatic activities across sectors, and facilitating political action by civil society organizations.  

### Surveillance {.unnumbered}
The second function, surveillance, addressed the group’s data needs. Members assessed what information was available, identified gaps, and designed collection efforts to address those gaps. Existing data were synthesized and summarized into formats that stakeholders could easily use, and when appropriate, these data were also released to the press to inform the broader public.  

### Health communication {.unnumbered}
The third function, health communication, involved both assessing communication needs and developing new materials in consultation with affected communities. At the same time, the group amplified and circulated materials that had been generated within communities themselves.  

### Resourcing {.unnumbered}
The final function, resourcing, supported the material needs of the other three. This meant identifying the resources required to sustain coordination, surveillance, and communication, and then mobilizing support from companies serving queer and trans communities, individual donors, private foundations, and from city, state, and federal governments.  

## Approach {.unnumbered}

### Project management {.unnumbered}
The group’s operational approach was both task-oriented and distributed. Teams developed structured task lists and assigned responsibilities to individuals. Each participant was empowered to track the status of their work, marking tasks as complete or pending, and reassigning them when necessary. Responsibilities were devolved with clear expectations, which ensured accountability while also preserving flexibility.  

### Coordination  {.unnumbered}
The group’s success depended not only on well-defined tasks but also on strong, distributed leadership. Leadership was not seen as a hierarchy but as a set of responsibilities shared across individuals who brought expertise, commitment, and perspective to the collective effort.  

The Principal Investigator anchored the group’s vision by building partnerships, guiding fundraising, drafting and reviewing study protocols, ensuring ethical oversight, and maintaining overall quality. The Research Coordinator worked closely with the Principal Investigator to sustain the rhythm of the group’s work by scheduling meetings, preparing technical documents, supporting research activities, and overseeing bookkeeping.  

The Communications Lead shaped how the group spoke to the world, managing newsletters, the website, attendance lists, and press engagement. The Questionnaire Lead designed data collection tools, integrated stakeholder feedback, and collaborated with the Translation Lead to ensure accessibility and inclusivity. The Translation Lead managed relationships with professional translators, conducted quality checks, and served as a bridge between technical experts and community voices.  

Digital infrastructure was guided by the Web Development Lead, who defined specifications for online tools and oversaw contracts with external developers. Together, these leaders ensured that the group remained scientifically rigorous, operationally efficient, and deeply connected to the communities it served.  


## Activities {.unnumbered}

### Investigator Meetings {.unnumbered}

Investigator meetings provided a regular space to review feedback from the Community Forum, monitor progress across different parts of the project, and align on overall timelines. They also preserved space for informal connection, which helped to strengthen trust and solidarity among members of the group.  

### Community Forum {.unnumbered}

In May 2022, the group launched the RESPND-MI LGBTQ+ Community Forum (CF) to support consultation and collective decision-making for a study on sexual activity and mpox symptoms. The CF quickly became a weekly space where activists, community leaders, and public health professionals shared updates, debated challenges, and shaped study design. Over the summer of 2022, more than 80 participants contributed to outputs such as policy briefs, op-eds, educational materials, and media outreach. The forum also influenced the study directly by requesting Spanish translation of materials, identifying key sites for outreach, and pressing for more inclusive communication that better represented transgender people. These contributions ensured that the study and the broader response were more responsive, equitable, and effective.  

### Talking to People and Making Things {.unnumbered}

Beyond formal structures, the group emphasized ongoing dialogue with communities and the rapid creation of tools, materials, and resources. This focus on listening, creating, and iterating was central to the group’s impact.  



### Dissemination {.unnumbered}

The group actively shared its work across local, national, and international platforms. Locally, members engaged with government departments and cultural venues, while nationally they contributed to forums such as the Choice Agenda. Globally, the group presented at major venues including the World Health Organization and the International AIDS Society conferences. Dissemination also included press engagement and academic presentations, which highlighted lessons from HIV/AIDS and connected them to the contemporary mpox response. Through these efforts, the group helped shape public dialogue, informed policy, and modeled how community-led initiatives could guide effective health emergency responses.
